nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1994 Jan 1. DMS|RGG; Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institution

note: There was no date on the original document so 1994 Jan 1 was assigned since most of the SLHs were prepared from 1994 thru 1997.

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name: Spanish sardine
Scientific Name: Sardinella aurita Valenciennes 1847
Classification: (Robins et. al. 1991).
	Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order: Clupeiformes
	Family: Clupeidae

Other Common Names: Gilt sardine

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  Harvested in schools along with O. oglinum and H. jaguana.  Sold as bait, cat food and for human consumption, with human consumption more common in Caribbean and eastern Atlantic areas (Ben-Tuvia 1960; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).

Recreational: Sold as bait (Shaw and Drullinger 1990).

Ecological Role: The abundant numbers, and biomass make the Spanish sardine an important component in the food chain as planktivore and as prey.  The juvenile are often found with O. oglinum and H. jaguana (Springer and Woodburn 1960; Christensen 1965; Low 1973) most widely distributed and common clupeid larvae (Shaw and Drullinger 1990).

Indicator:  None

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Circumtropical between 40 N and 30 S (Ben-Tuvia 1960).  Western Atlantic from Mass. to Uruguay, Gulf of Mexico and Caribbean to West Indies but most abundant in subtropical portion of its range (Shaw and Drullinger 1990, Klima 1971; Whitehead 1978; Robins et. al. 1986).

Within Study Area:  Abundant in the Indian River Lagoon near ocean inlets and adjacent continental shelf (Christensen 1965; Gilmore 1977, 1988)

Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Life Mode
nodes.body:
A planktivorous, nocturnal vertical migratory, coastal pelagic tropical species found usually in water less than 90-150 m in depth (Klima 1971; Ben-Tuvia 1971; Jones et. al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).
Movements and Migrations:  Migrates on a north-south gradient along the Atlantic  coast (Hildebrand 1963).  Nocturnal vertical migration as part of the deep scattering layer, also migrates onshore-offshore (Ben-Tuvia 1960; Schmidt 1972; Low 1973;  Jones et al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).  In Biscayne Bay there is a fall migration of  S. aurita southward along the coast (Low 1973). Mature fish remain in coastal waters during the fall migration (Low 1973).  In the Indian River Lagoon Spanish sardine are absent October-February  which corresponds with  movement to near shore spawning areas (Gilmore unpubl.).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  A common seagrass associate in the Indian River Lagoon (Gilmore 1988). Juveniles utilize seagrass beds as a  nursery for the first year (Low 197). Older individuals move into deeper water (Low 1973).

Substrate: Seagrass beds as juveniles, and nearshore open water as adults.

nodes.title: Physical/chemical
nodes.body:
Salinity: Found in high salinity areas usually above 33-34 ppt (Jones et. al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).
Temperature: Prefers temperatures above 18 C  (Ben-Tuvia 1960; Jones et. al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body:
Reproductive Mode: Gonochoristic, polygamous, oviparous, external fertilization, broadcast spawner,  pelagic spawner, iteroparous.
Mating/Spawning: Near shore pelagic spawning activity from late fall to spring with peaks in December-February (Houde and Fore 1973; Low 1973; Jones et. al 1978;  Fahay 1983; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).  Spawning occurs between 1930 and 2300 hrs with eggs found in the upper 10 m of the water column (Jones et. al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).  In the Indian River Lagoon Spanish sardine are absent October-February which corresponds with spawning  late fall to late spring (Gilmore unpubl.).   However, Herrema (1985) found evidence of spawning in May and August on the East coast of Florida.  In Brazil, Venezuela and the Mediterranean area, spawning occurs in the summer months (Ben-Tuvia 1960; Jones et. al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).  Prefers temperatures above 18 C and salinity above 34 ppt for spawning (Ben-Tuvia 1960; Jones et. al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).

Fecundity:  Western Atlantic and Gulf of Mexico populations batch fecundity varied in relation to size of female, 146 mm FL (21,240 ova) to  188 mm FL (146,729 ova), mean 70,312 eggs ( Jones et al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).  West African populations fecundity ranges 10,000 to 270,000 ova (Shaw and Drullinger 1990).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Egg:   Mean diameter 1.12 mm (Houde and Fore 1973) spherical, one oil droplet (mean 0.14mm) pelagic, found in the upper 10 m of the water column (Jones et. al. 1978; Shaw and Drullinger 1990).

Larvae:    Yolk sack larvae range from 2.3 to 4.06 mm (Jones et. al. 1978).  Hatching occurs around 3.0 mm (Fahay 1983).  Larvae range  from 3.0 mm to 7.0 mm, with the post larvae stage from 7.0 mm to 30 mm (Ben-Tuvia 1960).

Juvenile: At 30 days, 25-30 mm SL fish transform to juveniles (Ben-Tuvia 1960, Fahay 1983).  Juveniles as small as a 40 mm are captured in seagrass beds (Low 1973).

Adult:  Maturity can be reached in 2-3 years (Shaw and Drullinger 1990).  Mature individuals as small as 134 mm have been reported with the majority of the population mature at 190 mm (Low 1973).  Lifespan may be 6-7 years (Ben-Tuvia 1960).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Planktivorous with diet consisting mainly of copepods (Ben-Tuvia 1960; Hildebrand 1963; Böhlke and Chaplin 1968; Low 1973).

nodes.title: ECOLOGICAL INTERACTIONS
nodes.body:
Predation:  Found as prey for Scombroids, Istiophorids, Sphyraenids and Sciaenids (Ben-Tuvia 1960).  The abundant numbers, and biomass make the Spanish sardine an important component in the food chain as planktivore and as prey.

Other: Factors influencing populations include predation and fishing pressures.
